solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Striker effective only once in game given abuse

parts.note: a match is a game or contest
stick is informal for criticism or abuse, as in 'giving someone stick'

explanation.surface: A footballer who scored just once in a match takes a torrent of abuse from the crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Striker' looks like a footballer, but it is something struck to light, and it works only a single time.
explanation.definitionFit: A lucifer is struck against a box to light it and burns out after one use, so it is a single-use striker.

clue.text: Rag? It may come before the final exam

definitions.meaning: to rag someone is to tease or ridicule them

definitions.text: It may come before the final exam
definitions.meaning: a practice exam sat in advance of the real one

explanation.surface: A student newspaper, or rag, might be published ahead of finals.
explanation.definitionFit: To rag is to tease or deride; a trial exam taken before the real one is called by the same word.

clue.text: Male beast stifling cry when there's pain in paw

indicators.note: stifling means smothering, so one word holds the other within it

parts.note: a tup is a ram, a male sheep
ouch is what one cries when hurt

explanation.surface: An animal suppresses a yelp after hurting its foot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'paw' looks like part of the beast, but it is a verb, the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To paw someone is to fondle them unwelcomely, which is the informal British sense of the phrasal verb.

clue.text: Like Santa's deliveries, ho-ho!

parts.note: HO is the standard abbreviation for house, so 'ho-ho' reads as one HO then another: ho to ho

explanation.surface: Father Christmas laughs his famous laugh while making his rounds.
explanation.walkthrough: The hyphenated laugh is read as HO followed by HO, each standing for 'house', joined by the hyphen as 'to'.
explanation.definitionFit: Santa calls at every home in turn on Christmas Eve, going door by door down each street.

clue.text: Journey with urgent message? The enemy could lay this trap

definitions.text: The enemy could lay this trap

parts.note: a trip is a journey
a wire is a telegram, the old way of sending an urgent message

explanation.surface: A traveller receives an urgent telegram warning of an enemy ambush.
explanation.definitionFit: A low concealed cable that sets off a mine or alarm when snagged is a trap an enemy might set.

clue.text: Snappily kinky, with little time to get involved

indicators.note: getting involved means being drawn into the middle, so the small piece goes inside

parts.note: kinky hair is curly
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: Someone describes a quick kinky encounter in a snappy way.
explanation.definitionFit: Speaking snappily means answering in a brusque, short manner, which is what the adverb describes.

clue.text: Former Yugoslav leader not half an obnoxious person

indicators.note: dropping half means only the first four of the name's eight letters are kept

parts.note: Slobodan Milosevic was the former leader of Yugoslavia

explanation.surface: A disparaging verdict on a Balkan politician as only half decent, or rather obnoxious.
explanation.walkthrough: The leader's first name is used, not his surname.
explanation.definitionFit: A lazy, untidy, unpleasant individual is called by this informal word of contempt.

clue.text: 'Acid' in clue wrongly associated with 'drug'?

indicators.note: wrongly means the letters are put in the wrong order, rearranged

parts.note: E is ecstasy, the drug

explanation.surface: A pedant objects that 'acid' in a crossword was wrongly matched with 'drug'.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Acid' looks like the slang for LSD, which is why the surface pairs it with 'drug', but it is the definition: an amino acid. 'wrongly' rearranges IN CLUE into LEUCIN.
explanation.definitionFit: This is one of the essential amino acids found in proteins, so it is an example of an acid.

clue.text: Brat grew troublesome, concealing identity in West Country town

indicators.note: concealing means hiding within, so the shuffled letters wrap around the short piece
troublesome suggests the letters are unruly and must be rearranged

parts.note: ID is the usual short form of identity

explanation.surface: A naughty child acting up while hiding who they are in a Somerset town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'troublesome' turns BRAT GREW into BRGWATER, and 'concealing' puts ID inside it. The West Country is England's south-west.
explanation.definitionFit: This market town lies in Somerset, a county in the south-west of England.

clue.text: They design tour, cruise at sea

indicators.note: at sea means confused or all over the place, so the letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: Fashion people plan a trip on a cruise ship.
explanation.definitionFit: These are high-fashion dressmakers, people who create and design clothes.

clue.text: Language of one place to the west

indicators.note: in an across clue going to the west means running right to left, backwards

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one
to put is to place

explanation.surface: A language spoken in a single western region.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to the west' turns I PUT round to give the letters in the grid.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a South American indigenous tongue spoken in Brazil and Paraguay.

clue.text: Suffer maybe after dreadful Ofsted inspection and go crazy

definitions.text: Suffer maybe after dreadful Ofsted inspection
definitions.meaning: a failing school may be left without its headteacher; Ofsted is the English schools inspectorate
to panic or lose all composure

explanation.surface: A school goes to pieces after a damning government inspection.
explanation.walkthrough: Read literally, the first part is a school that ends up without its headteacher; Ofsted is the body that inspects schools in England.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to lose self-control and panic; taken literally, a school whose head is sacked suffers exactly that.

clue.text: That's exciting turn that shouldn't finish!

indicators.note: shouldn't finish means the word loses its final letter

parts.note: to wheel is to turn

explanation.surface: A thrill-seeker on a ride begging for the spin not to end.
explanation.definitionFit: It is an exclamation of delight or excitement, as on a fairground ride.

clue.text: See everyone work in side as the result of heavy defeat

indicators.note: in places the first two pieces inside the word for side

parts.note: a wing is a side, as of a building or team
all means everyone
OP is short for opus, a work

explanation.surface: A team suffers a hammering after everyone works on the flank.
explanation.walkthrough: 'See' is only a pointer to what follows.
explanation.definitionFit: A thrashing or crushing loss, in informal use, is the same as a severe beating.

clue.text: Angry PM no longer seen in one part of London

parts.note: black can mean angry or threatening, as in black looks
Edward Heath was a British Prime Minister of the 1970s

explanation.surface: A furious former prime minister has vanished somewhere in London.
explanation.walkthrough: Heath was UK Prime Minister 1970 to 1974.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a district of south-east London known for its large open common, so it is one area of the city.

clue.text: Support for someone sitting down to drink, having got fed up, we hear

parts.note: to lap is to drink, as a cat does

indicators.note: we hear signals a word that sounds like another

parts.note: bored means fed up

explanation.surface: Someone sits down for a drink because they are fed up.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a flat panel resting on the knees, used as a desk or tray by a seated person.

clue.text: Dope takes road in the wrong direction in city

parts.note: gen and dope are both slang for information

indicators.note: the wrong direction for an across entry is backwards

parts.note: AVE is short for avenue, a road

explanation.surface: A drug addict drives the wrong way down a road in a city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dope' looks like drugs, but it means information.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a Swiss city on its lake, home to many international organisations.

clue.text: A bit from the likes of Steptoe and Son wrapped in paper

indicators.note: wrapped in means enclosed by, so one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: FT is the Financial Times newspaper

parts.words: the likes of Steptoe and Son
parts.note: Steptoe and Son, a British TV sitcom, was about rag-and-bone men, scrap collectors

explanation.surface: Scrap dealers wrap a scrap in newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: Steptoe and Son was a 1960s-70s British sitcom about a father and son who collected junk with a horse and cart.
explanation.definitionFit: A small broken-off piece of something is a bit of it.

clue.text: Shelter in which short drink's feasible

indicators.note: short means a word loses its last letter

parts.note: cocoa is a hot drink
on means possible or feasible, as in 'that's not on'

explanation.surface: A cosy hideaway where a quick nip of something is allowed.
explanation.definitionFit: A silk case spun by a larva protects it, and figuratively any protective enclosure.

clue.text: Certain precautions needed in admirable arrangement to cut down journeys

indicators.note: needed in says the short piece must go inside the other

parts.note: cool is slang for admirable or impressive
ARP stands for Air Raid Precautions, the British wartime civil defence service

explanation.surface: Commuters praise an admirable safety-conscious plan to reduce travel.
explanation.walkthrough: ARP is Air Raid Precautions from Second World War Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: Sharing car rides among colleagues reduces the number of separate trips made, which is exactly what this scheme is for.

clue.text: As an erstwhile statesman, I dance when going round the country

indicators.note: going round means surrounding, so the dance encloses the country

parts.note: a ronde is a round dance
UK is the United Kingdom

explanation.surface: A former politician dances around his homeland.
explanation.walkthrough: The nickname belongs to the Duke of Wellington, who was a general and later Prime Minister.
explanation.definitionFit: Wellington, victor at Waterloo and later Prime Minister, was nicknamed this, so he is a former statesman.

clue.text: Actor given break, heading off on All Saints' Day

indicators.note: heading off means the first letter is removed

parts.note: to bust is to break
All Saints' Day falls on 1 November, written 1 NOV, with 1 as I

explanation.surface: An actor gets his big break on the first of November.
explanation.walkthrough: All Saints' Day is 1 November; the 1 becomes I to give INOV.
explanation.definitionFit: Peter Ustinov was a celebrated British actor, writer and raconteur, so the surname names a performer.

clue.text: Fixed penalty for smuggling in drink

indicators.note: smuggling in means secretly taking something inside, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: a fine is a penalty
It is gin and It, Italian vermouth, a drink

explanation.surface: A set penalty for bringing alcohol across a border.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fixed penalty' reads as one phrase, but 'Fixed' is the definition. 'It' is Italian vermouth, as in gin and It.
explanation.definitionFit: Something limited and bounded rather than endless has fixed limits; the adjective means exactly that.

clue.text: Annoying idiot's rushing around

indicators.note: around means the outer word goes round the inner

parts.note: haring means rushing, running like a hare
an ass is an idiot

explanation.surface: A fool dashing about is getting on someone's nerves.
explanation.definitionFit: Pestering someone persistently is being troublesome or irritating to them.

clue.text: One of the earliest fellows to be a famous author

definitions.meaning: in Genesis, the third son of Adam and Eve, among the first men
Vikram ... is the author of A Suitable Boy

explanation.surface: One of the earliest men destined to become a famous writer.
explanation.definitionFit: The biblical third son of Adam shares his name with Vikram, the Indian novelist.

clue.text: Accordingly, one day of the week's not right day

indicators.note: not says the following pieces are left out of the weekday

parts.note: Thursday is a day of the week
taken as written

explanation.surface: A weekday that is not a proper day, so to speak.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words mean 'therefore' or 'consequently', introducing a result.

clue.text: Swear nothing's been hidden in a car

indicators.note: hidden in means placed inside, so one piece goes into the other

parts.note: VW is a Volkswagen car
O is zero, nothing

explanation.surface: Someone vows that nothing has been concealed in the vehicle.
explanation.definitionFit: To declare something solemnly and openly is to assert or affirm it, as one does when swearing.

clue.text: Fancy hotel (e'en the inn!) is where one might get a drink

definitions.text: where one might get a drink

indicators.note: fancy means elaborate or fanciful, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A smart hotel or even the inn is a place for a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fancy' looks like an adjective for the hotel, but it rearranges HOTEL EEN THE INN. Golf courses have eighteen holes, so the next one is the clubhouse bar.
explanation.definitionFit: Golfers jokingly call the clubhouse bar by this name, the place they go to drink after eighteen holes.

clue.text: See 27
Actress laid down with divine male, rolling over

parts.note: to lay down a bet is to wager, so laid down means betted

indicators.note: rolling over means turning round, so the god's name is read backwards

parts.note: Siva, or Shiva, is a male Hindu god

explanation.surface: An actress lay down beside a godlike man who was rolling over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'laid' suggests lying down, but it means wagered.
explanation.definitionFit: The star of All About Eve was one of Hollywood's great leading ladies.
